title: Resting the Mind and Severing Delusion
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Zhong Mingxing of Chaling, born of a family versed in poetry and ritual, once fled to Guangdong on account of calamity and sought me out at Caoxi. The old master explained to him the doctrine of retribution for good and evil and the law of cause and effect, and set his mind at rest before he returned; in the end his misfortune was resolved. The way of that resolution was something no recollection could reach: a chance accord of circumstances, arriving of itself with no intent. From that time his property was preserved intact, and he stepped into a state of serene unconcern. Yet he could not fathom whence it came.

inline.s: (From the Dream Wanderings Collection:
Admonition to Zhong Hengying

Zhong Mingxing of Chaling, born of a family versed in poetry and ritual, once fled to Guangdong on account of calamity and sought me out at Caoxi. The old master set forth to him the doctrine of retribution for good and evil and the law of cause and effect, and set his mind at rest before he went home, and his trouble was indeed dissolved. What dissolved it was something no memory could reach: a chance accord of circumstances, arriving of itself with no thought on his part. From that time his possessions were left unscathed, and he entered a state of serene unconcern. And yet he remained wholly at a loss as to why it had been dissolved, still scheming after the fame and wealth of a lifetime he had never won, resolved to exhaust his mind and strength in pursuing them as though he had but to reach into a bag or stoop for a blade of grass.

Zhong of Chaling (a place name), whose style name was Mingxing, was raised in a household renowned for poetry and ritual. Formerly, fleeing calamity, he travelled to Guangdong and paid his respects to the old master (Hanshan Deqing's own designation) at Caoxi. The old master explained the doctrine of retribution for good and evil and the law of cause and effect; his mind was set at rest, and upon his return his misfortune had in the end dissolved. That it dissolved was not something deliberate foresight could have reached: it came of its own accord through a chance meeting of circumstances. Zhong's household property was thereupon preserved intact, and he entered into a state of tranquil ease, free of entanglements. Yet he still did not know why the calamity had been dispelled; he continued to scheme after the fame, rank, and wealth he had never achieved in life (the things that delighted and satisfied the heart), resolved to spend his mind and strength in pursuing them, believing it as easy as fetching from a bag or stooping for a blade of grass.

[Fetching from a bag, stooping for a blade of grass] Taking something out of a bag, or bending down to pick a blade of grass, metaphors for a task that can be accomplished with the greatest ease. Bag: a pocket or a sack. Grass: a tiny blade.

On the last day of the year of Jiayin, together with Liu Cunzhi, a friend who had come from afar to comfort me, I was accompanied through the old year. The old master sighed and said: What you purpose, sir, is to cross the seas and ford the rivers in search of a sweet spring to drink. Not only is the spring unlikely to be reached, but your thirst burns the fiercer, and you weary yourself in vain with the toil of the journey. Once I explained to you the principle of retribution and cause and effect, have you forgotten it? For the response of good and evil is swift as echo and shadow: when the sound is harmonious the echo answers in kind, and when the form is upright the shadow is straight. Therefore the sage does not speak openly of cause and effect, but only says, 'Do good and a hundred blessings descend upon you; do evil and a hundred calamities.' Thus he admonishes us to accept our lot and fix our resolve. Hence it is said: 'One who does not understand the decree cannot be called a man of noble character.'

On the eve of the New Year in the Jiayin year, Liu Cunzhi came from afar to console me, and together we saw out the old year. The old master heaved a sigh and said: Your plan, sir, is like crossing seas and fording rivers to find a sweet spring to quench your thirst. The spring may not be found, while your thirst burns only more fiercely, and you suffer in vain the toil of that long journey. Once I admonished you with the principle of cause and retribution, have you forgotten it all the while? In the interplay of good and evil the retribution is swift as a shadow following a form or an echo answering a sound. When the sound is harmonious, the echo answers in tune; when the form is upright, the shadow is straight. Hence the sages, though they do not speak openly of cause and effect, say that 'doing good brings down a hundred blessings, and doing evil brings down a hundred calamities,' and so they enjoin us to accept our lot and settle our resolve. Hence it is said: 'Without knowing the decree, one cannot be a gentleman.'

The sage teaches men to accept their lot; the Buddha teaches men to accord with conditions. Their Way is one. If one accepts his lot, not a single thing need be forced; if one accords with conditions, not a single thought may be given to vain imagining. Therefore the Buddha's teaching makes the severing of delusion its very root, for delusion is the root of all the evil karma of greed, hatred, and ignorance. Even the bodhisattva's cultivation leading to buddhahood, and the most sublime, majestic, and vast field of merit reaped in heavens and among men, all begin with the severing of delusion. When delusion is severed, evil karma is extinguished; when evil karma is extinguished, a hundred blessings gather, and this is what is meant by seeking much blessing for oneself.

The sage teaches us to accept our lot; the World-Honoured One teaches us to accord with conditions. Their principle is one and the same. To accept one's lot: not the slightest thing need be done by force. To accord with conditions: not a single thought may fall into vain imagining. Therefore the Buddha's teaching takes the severing of delusion as its foundation, for delusion is the root of the manifold evil karma of greed, hatred, and ignorance. Even the bodhisattva's practice and final attainment of buddhahood, and the vast field of supreme and majestic merit reaped in heaven and among men, all begin with the severing of delusion. When delusion is severed, evil karma dissolves; when evil karma dissolves, a hundred blessings assemble, and this is what is meant by seeking much blessing for oneself.
[Seeking much blessing for oneself] The Book of Songs says:
"Ever mindful of the decree, seek much blessing for yourself."

(The Book of Songs says: ever in accord with Heaven's decree, seek much blessing for yourself.) [Ever mindful of the decree] Always conforming to Heaven's decree. [Ever] always, at all times. [Mindful] a particle of speech carrying no independent meaning. [Conform] to accord with. [Decree] the mandate of Heaven.

Therefore he revealed to him this gatha: "All worldly affairs arise from delusion; where the deluded mind dissolves, the karmic bonds grow light. There is no need to seek the path of bodhi elsewhere; one has only to take a step backward." To step back, to cease clinging and to stop seeking, is the foremost practice of resting the mind and severing delusion. Because the human mind is originally bright and vast, the source of ten thousand blessings; yet because it is veiled by delusion and evil karma, calamities daily arise while blessings daily decline. Now if delusion dissolves and karma is severed, then the one nature becomes perfectly luminous and its enjoyment is boundless; where this enjoyment is obtained, that is true blessing. Thus one knows that blessing is brought about by oneself,
(the character zheng, here the same as 'just')
and is by no means attainable through craft, wit, or deceit. Moreover, the Buddha taught that by severing the deluded mind one stirs the blessings of the human and heavenly realms.

Therefore he revealed to him this gatha: "All worldly affairs arise from delusion; where the deluded mind dissolves, the karmic bonds grow light. There is no need to seek the path of bodhi elsewhere; one has only to take a step backward." To step back (not to cling, not to pursue) is the supreme practice of resting the mind and severing delusion. Because the human mind is originally bright and vast, the fountainhead of ten thousand blessings; yet because it is obscured by delusion and evil karma, calamities daily increase while blessings daily diminish. If now delusion dissolves and karma is severed, then the one nature is wholly luminous and its enjoyment is without bound; where enjoyment is thus obtained, that is true blessing. Therefore one knows that blessing is created by oneself, and can in no way be gained by cunning or clever scheming. Moreover, the Buddha teaches that when the deluded mind is severed, one wins the blessings of the human and heavenly realms.
[Resting the mind and severing delusion] To bring to rest the mind that clings and seeks, and to cut off vain imaginings.

Zhong possesses the native talent for fame, rank, and wealth. If he can straightway rest his mind, and take the deeds of his whole former life and examine them one by one carefully from the very beginning, then wherever there is a single thought that wrongs his conscience or harms principle and accords not with the Great Way, all of it is a root of suffering; let him cast it out at once. Then, founding a new root, let him set to work anew, holding to the single matter of "resting the mind and severing delusion, accepting the decree and awaiting the season" as his standard, and concentrating on the undertakings that are inherently his own, without seeking any other matter of vain imagining. In this way he repairs the losses of his former conduct.

Zhong already possesses the talent and strategy for fame, rank, and wealth. If he can straightway still his mind, and take up the deeds of his whole former life and examine them one by one carefully from the beginning, then whatever single thought has wronged his conscience, harmed principle, or disaccorded with the Great Way is entirely a root of suffering: let him discard it all at once. Let him found a new root and pursue a different line of effort, concentrating on this one matter of "resting the mind and severing delusion, accepting the decree and awaiting the season," taking it as the standard of his thought and action, and applying himself to the work that is inherently his own, without seeking any separate matter of vain imagining; such is the way to make good the faults of his former conduct.
[The compound zi ji] means talent and strategy. [The character si
(pronounced si),
means to wait.

Once the calamity has vanished and blessing arrives, then fame, rank, and wealth come pressing upon him, and there is no place to evade them. Why then must he seek them by means of manifold delusion and clinging? If Zhong can truly believe without a doubt, and take up this practice and carry it out, then the fruit of buddhahood may be hoped for, how much more the mundane conditions of the world? Strive on! Strive on!

Once the calamity is dispelled and blessing arrives, fame, rank, and wealth press close upon you; even if you wished to evade them, there would be no place to evade them. Why then must you pursue them through manifold vain imaginings and clinging? (This is to say: blessing is not something to be won by delusion and clinging, but must be attained by severing the roots of suffering and cultivating the causes of blessing. Once the causes of blessing come to fruit, the reward descends of itself.) If Zhong can truly believe without doubt, and hold to this and practice it, then the fruit of buddhahood may be hoped for, how much more so the fame, rank, and wealth of this world? Strive on! Strive on!
